title: The Day of Atonement
summary: After the death of Aaron's two sons, God tells Moses how and when Aaron may enter the Most Holy Place: once a year, dressed in plain linen, with blood and a cloud of incense. Aaron purifies the sanctuary with the blood of a bull and a goat, then confesses Israel's sins over a second, living goat and sends it into the wilderness. The day becomes a permanent annual fast and Sabbath for all Israel.
story: The chapter opens by reaching back to Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire and died before the LORD. That disaster raised the question the whole book has been circling: how can a holy God live in the middle of a sinful, impure people without consuming them? Chapters 11 to 15 dealt with the uncleanness of daily life, from food to skin disease to bodily discharges. Chapter 16 gathers up everything those laws could not reach, the impurity and rebellion that build up over a year and cling to the sanctuary itself, and deals with it in one great annual cleansing. It stands near the center of Leviticus, and it is the hinge between the laws of purity before it and the call to holy living in chapters 17 to 27.
historical:
Leviticus presents these instructions as given at Mount Sinai in the year after the exodus, while Israel camped around the newly built tabernacle, the portable tent-sanctuary described in Exodus 25 to 40. As with the rest of the Pentateuch (the first five books of the Bible), the date of writing is debated. Tradition credits the material to Moses. Many modern scholars assign Leviticus 1 to 16 to a priestly source compiled during or after the Babylonian exile in the sixth century BC, while others argue that its rituals are much older and fit the world of the second millennium BC. The ritual itself was practiced for centuries. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200, devotes a whole tractate (Yoma, Aramaic for the Day) to how the day was kept in the Second Temple, including the report that the goat was led to a ravine in the desert and pushed over the edge. The book of Acts calls the season simply the Fast (Acts 27:9).

Israel's neighbors also had rites for cleansing temples and carrying evil away. In the Babylonian New Year festival, a priest purified a shrine by wiping it with the carcass of a slaughtered ram, which was then thrown into the river, and the men who handled it had to stay out of the city until the festival ended. Hittite texts from Anatolia describe rituals in which an animal was driven off toward enemy territory to carry a plague away. Leviticus 16 shares the basic idea that impurity can be removed physically, but it has no incantations, no demons to appease, and no magic: everything is done because the LORD commanded it, and the goat carries confessed sin, not disease.
cultural:
For a first reader the tabernacle was a house with rooms of rising holiness: the courtyard with its altar, the Holy Place with its lampstand and table, and behind a thick curtain the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood and God's presence appeared above its gold lid, the mercy seat. Ordinary priests served daily in the Holy Place. No one entered the inner room except the high priest, and only on this day. He did not wear the jeweled breastpiece and gold-trimmed robes of Exodus 28 but a plain linen tunic, sash, and turban, more like a servant's dress, and he bathed before putting it on. The cloud of incense hid the mercy seat so that he would not see God and die.

The chapter assumes that sin and impurity do not stay with the sinner. They pollute the place where God dwells, the way smoke stains a house. The blood sprinkled on and before the mercy seat, in the tent, and on the altar cleanses those places from "the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites" (verse 16). Then the second goat deals with the people's guilt itself. The instruction that the people "humble yourselves" (verse 29) was understood as fasting, and the day was the only fast required by the law of Moses. It applied to native Israelites and resident foreigners alike.
literary: The chapter is a ritual text, written as instruction. It first lists what Aaron must bring and wear (verses 3 to 5), then gives a quick summary of the rite (verses 6 to 10), and only then walks through it slowly (verses 11 to 28), moving outward from the Most Holy Place to the tent, then to the altar, then beyond the camp. The word for making atonement appears sixteen times and binds the whole text together. The closing paragraph (verses 29 to 34) turns from the priest to the people and fixes the date, repeating three times that this is "a permanent statute". The final line, "And all this was done as the LORD had commanded Moses", marks obedience, the opposite of what Nadab and Abihu did.

outline.t: A warning after the death of Aaron's sons
What Aaron must bring and wear
The bull and the two goats, chosen by lot
Blood inside the veil: cleansing the sanctuary and the altar
The live goat carries the people's sins away
Washing, burnt offerings, and burning outside the camp
A permanent statute for the tenth day of the seventh month

doctrines.note: The chapter shows atonement in two movements: blood that cleanses what sin has defiled, and a goat that carries confessed guilt away. Both are God's provision, not Israel's bargaining. The result is stated in verse 30: the people are made clean from all their sins before the LORD.

God's presence is a gift that can kill. Access to him is real but ordered: one man, one day, one room, in the right clothes and with the right blood. Holiness here is not fussiness but the reality of who God is.

The text names sin with several words: impurities, rebellious acts, iniquities, and sins (verses 16 and 21). Sin is not only an act that is over once it is done; it leaves a stain on the community and the place of worship that has to be dealt with.

words.note: Kipper, to make atonement. The meaning of the verb is debated. Some link it to covering, others to wiping clean or purging (as with an Akkadian cognate used for ritual cleansing), and others to the related noun for a ransom price paid to spare a life. In this chapter the objects of the verb include places (the sanctuary, the tent, the altar) as well as people, which suggests cleansing is central, but rescue from deserved death is never far away.

Kapporet, the mercy seat or atonement cover: the gold lid of the ark, with the two cherubim above it, where God appeared. The word shares a root with kipper. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, rendered it with hilasterion, the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25, where the BSB has "atoning sacrifice".

Azazel, the name given to the second goat's destination. Its meaning is disputed. It has been read as a description of the goat itself, the goat that goes away (the reading behind the English word scapegoat, coined by William Tyndale in 1530), as a place name for a rugged cliff in the desert, as an abstract term for complete removal, or as the name of a wilderness spirit, a reading found in later Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch. On any reading, the goat is not an offering to Azazel; only the LORD receives sacrifice here.

Chattat, the sin offering. The same word means sin, and the offering is named for what it deals with. Jacob Milgrom and others have argued it is better called a purification offering, since its blood cleanses the sanctuary from the effects of sin and impurity. That is exactly what it does in verses 15 to 19.

christ: The letter to the Hebrews reads Jesus' work directly through this chapter. It recalls that "only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood" (Hebrews 9:7), and then says that Christ "entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption" (Hebrews 9:12). Where Aaron needed a bull for his own sin first, Hebrews presents Jesus as a sinless priest who offered himself. The bodies of the sin offerings burned outside the camp become, in Hebrews 13:11-12, a picture of Jesus who "suffered outside the city gate". Christians have also seen in the living goat a picture of sin carried away, which fits the language of Isaiah 53, though the New Testament does not make that link explicitly. The veil that barred everyone but the high priest becomes, in Hebrews 10:19-20, the way opened for all through Christ's body.

hard.q: How could the blood of animals, or a goat sent into the desert, really deal with human guilt?
hard.a: The question is old; the New Testament raises it itself, saying "it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins" (Hebrews 10:4). Modern readers often see the ritual as a primitive transfer of guilt, like magic. Jewish interpreters have long answered that the rite never worked apart from repentance: the people fasted and humbled themselves, and later rabbinic teaching held that the day atones only for those who turn back to God, and that wrongs against a neighbor require making things right with the neighbor first. Christian interpreters generally agree that the animals had no power in themselves. Leviticus 17:11 says the blood atones because God has given it for that purpose. On the Christian reading, the Day of Atonement was God's real provision for Israel's life with him in its time, and also a picture pointing ahead to a sacrifice that could do fully what the annual rite could only signify. Many Jewish readers, by contrast, see the rite as complete in its own terms, and after the temple's destruction in AD 70 they kept the day through prayer, fasting, and repentance.

questions: The chapter treats sin as something that stains a whole community and its place of worship, not only the individual. Where do you see the effects of wrongdoing spreading beyond the person who did it?
Aaron had to make atonement for himself before he could do it for anyone else. What does that say about the people we trust to lead us spiritually?
The live goat carried confessed sins far away. What would it mean for you to believe that a wrong you have confessed is truly gone?
